qs.q: A 22-year-old man presents with a fluctuant swelling along the lower third of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Imaging confirms a second branchial arch anomaly. Which of the following describes the typical course of its tract relative to surrounding neck structures?
o: Runs over carotid sheath and hypoglossal nerve
Ascends deep into posterior triangle of neck
Passes directly through the parotid gland tissue
Pierces central hyoid bone to terminate blindly
qs.e: The second branchial arch anomaly tract runs over the carotid sheath and hypoglossal nerve, and between the internal and external carotid arteries. First arch anomalies relate to the parotid gland and facial nerve, not second arch tracts.
qs.s: Neck Masses: Assessment, Congenital Lumps, Lymph Nodes and Salivary: MCQs

qs.q: A 42-year-old man presents with a soft, fluctuant swelling anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle that appeared after an upper respiratory tract infection. What is the most critical initial management step given his age?
o: Urgent simple needle drainage of the fluid
Fine-needle aspiration and head and neck examination
Direct incision and primary closure in the clinic
qs.e: A cystic mass in the upper neck in an adult over 40 may represent a cystic nodal metastasis, making FNA and a full head and neck examination mandatory. Simple drainage should be avoided as it can complicate subsequent procedures.
qs.s: Neck Masses: Assessment, Congenital Lumps, Lymph Nodes and Salivary: MCQs

qs.q: A 7‑year‑old presents with a draining sinus along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid that ascends toward the tonsillar fossa, consistent with a second branchial cleft anomaly. Which hereditary syndrome should be screened for in this patient?
qs.e: Second branchial cleft anomalies are classically associated with branchio‑oto‑renal disorder, which warrants renal imaging. The other conditions are unrelated genetic syndromes that do not feature branchial cleft anomalies.
qs.s: Neck Masses: Assessment, Congenital Lumps, Lymph Nodes and Salivary: MCQs

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The sternocleidomastoid is a paired neck muscle that flexes and rotates the head, and its dysfunction can mimic airway obstruction or neurological deficits. Recognizing its anatomy helps diagnose neck masses, torticollis, and airway compromise.

sections.p: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is a superficial, strap‑like muscle that runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process. It is a key landmark for airway management and a common site for branchial cysts.
The SCM lies in the lateral neck, superficial to the carotid sheath. It is easily palpated by turning the head and can be visualized on ultrasound in low‑resource settings.
b: Anterior border of SCM is a common site for branchial cysts

sections.p: Posterior to the SCM is the carotid sheath containing the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The SCM overlies the sternocleidomastoid fascia and the platysma.
Supplied by the occipital artery (posterior branch) and the superior thyroid artery (anterior branch). These vessels are often visualized on Doppler ultrasound.
Motor innervation is via the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) and the cervical plexus (C2–C4). Sensory input is minimal.
The SCM flexes the neck, rotates the head to the opposite side, and, when both sides contract, elevates the sternum during forced inspiration.
Torticollis, SCM strain, and branchial cysts are common. SCM hypertrophy can indicate airway obstruction or a mass effect on the trachea.
b: SCM strain – acute pain after trauma

sections.p: Ask the patient to turn the head; a unilateral SCM contraction indicates a possible accessory nerve lesion. In airway emergencies, palpate the SCM to locate the trachea.
b: SCM contraction on head turn = accessory nerve integrity

whenToSeekHelp: Severe neck pain with swelling, sudden airway obstruction, or neurological deficits such as weakness or dysphagia

faq.q: What causes SCM pain after a fall?
faq.a: Direct trauma or hyperextension can strain the muscle, leading to localized pain and limited neck movement.

faq.q: Can a branchial cyst mimic a tumor?
faq.a: Yes, a cyst on the SCM’s anterior border can appear as a mass; imaging distinguishes it from malignancy.

faq.q: Why is the SCM important in intubation?
faq.a: It marks the trachea’s midline; over‑extension can pull the trachea laterally, complicating intubation.
